pious.path: Latin pius described someone who fulfilled their duty to gods, family, and country. English kept the devout sense, but also the ironic edge: a pious display of duty can look performed rather than felt, hence sanctimonious.

piquant.path: French piquer meant to prick or sting like a pin. A piquant flavor stings the tongue pleasantly, and by extension a piquant remark or story has that same sharp, lively bite.

pique.path: French pique named a literal prick or sting, and figuratively the stinging feeling of a wounded ego. To feel pique is to feel pricked in one's pride.

parts.meaning: central strand of a plant stem

pith.literal: the spongy center of a stalk
pith.path: Pith first named the soft tissue at the center of a plant stem. Because that core held the plant together, pith came to mean the essential heart of any matter.

pithy.path: Pithy grew directly from pith, the compact core of a stalk. A pithy remark is packed with meaning the way pith fills a stem, with nothing wasted.

pittance.path: A pittance was originally a small allowance of food or alms given to monks or the poor out of piety. Because such gifts were meager, the word came to mean any skimpy amount of money.

placate.path: Latin placare meant to smooth something over, related to placere, to please. To placate someone is to calm their anger the way you'd calm rough water.

placebo.path: Placebo is Latin for 'I shall please,' the opening word of a psalm sung in the medieval service for the dead. Because mourners were paid to sing it, the word came to mean a flatterer, and later a treatment given only to please or humor a patient.

placid.path: Latin placidus described whatever was calm and undisturbed, like a still pond, related to placere, to please.

parts.meaning: to strike, lament, beat the breast

plaintive.path: Latin plangere meant to strike, specifically to beat one's chest in mourning. A plaintive sound still carries that note of lamentation.

plastic.path: Greek plassein meant to shape or mold, the way a sculptor works clay. Something plastic can be reshaped freely without breaking.

plasticity.path: Built on the same root as plastic, plasticity names the capacity to be shaped or to adapt, whether in materials, the brain, or a plan.

platitude.path: French plat means flat. A platitude is a 'flat' remark, one worn smooth by overuse, with no freshness or elevation left in it.

plausible.path: Latin plausibilis meant deserving applause, praiseworthy. A plausible claim originally won approval outright; now it just seems believable enough to accept at a glance, even if false.

parts.meaning: a decree, thing agreed upon (from placere, to please)

plead.path: Latin placitum meant a decision or ruling, literally a thing 'pleasing' or agreed upon. Old French turned this into pleading a case in court, and English broadened it to arguing or begging earnestly for anything.

plebeian.path: In Rome the plebs were ordinary citizens, as opposed to the patrician nobility. Plebeian came to describe anything common or lacking refinement.

plenitude.path: Latin plenus meant full or complete. Plenitude is simply a state of fullness, an abundant supply.

plethora.path: Greek plethore first named a medical condition of having too much blood, an overfullness. The word broadened to mean any excessive amount of anything.

pliant.path: Latin plicare meant to fold. Something pliant bends and folds easily, whether cloth bending in the hand or a person's will bending under pressure.

plod.path: Plod is of uncertain origin, likely imitative of the dull sound of trudging feet. It has always meant to walk or work slowly and doggedly.

plodding.path: Built from plod, itself likely an imitation of trudging footsteps, plodding describes work or movement that is slow and unimaginative but steady.

ploy.path: Ploy's origin is genuinely uncertain: it may be a clipped form of employ, or linked to deploy. The modern sense of a cunning tactic only became common in the 20th century.

plucky.path: Pluck first named the heart and innards of a slaughtered animal, the parts pulled out. By the 1800s pluck had come to mean courage or spirit, and plucky described someone who showed it.

plumb.literal: to measure with a lead weight
plumb.path: A plumb line was a cord weighted with lead, used to measure depth or check vertical alignment. To plumb something is to sound its depths the way sailors used a lead weight to measure water.

parts.meaning: sounding lead, plumb line (from plom, lead)

plummet.literal: to drop like a lead weight
plummet.path: A plummet was originally a small lead weight used like a plumb line. Because such a weight drops straight down fast, the word became a verb for falling steeply and suddenly.

plus.path: Latin plus simply meant 'more.' English borrowed it first as the addition sign, then as a noun for an added benefit, an advantage.

plutocracy.path: Greek ploutos meant wealth and kratos meant power. A plutocracy is government run by, and for, the rich.

podium.path: Greek podion, a 'little foot,' named a raised base or pedestal. Latin podium extended this to an elevated platform, the podium a speaker stands on.

poignancy.path: Built on Latin pungere, to prick or stab, poignancy is the quality of an experience that pierces you emotionally, a sharp sting of feeling.

poignant.path: Latin pungere meant to prick or stab. A poignant memory or scene pierces you emotionally, a sharp sting that is often sad.

poise.path: Poise comes from an Old French word for weight, itself from Latin pendere, to weigh or hang in balance. A poised person carries themselves evenly, weighted and steady.

polarize.path: Greek polos named the axis a sphere turns on, giving us the North and South poles. To polarize a group is to push its members toward two opposite extremes.

polarized.path: From the same root as pole, polarized describes a group or opinion that has split apart into two opposing extremes.

polemic.path: Greek polemos meant war. A polemic treats argument as combat, a fierce written or spoken attack rather than a calm debate.

polemical.path: Sharing its root with polemic and Greek polemos, war, polemical describes writing or speech that attacks its target combatively rather than reasoning calmly.

policy.path: Greek polis meant city-state, and politeia was its governance. Policy narrowed to a deliberate course of action a government or organization adopts to manage its affairs.

politic.path: From the same root as politics, the art of running a city, politic describes behavior that is prudent and shrewd about the circumstances, the way a skilled statesman would act.

polity.path: Sharing its root with policy and politics, polity names an organized political community with its own system of government.

parts.meaning: title character of Eleanor Porter's 1913 novel

pollyannaish.path: Pollyanna was the heroine of a 1913 novel, famous for finding something to be glad about in every misfortune. Pollyannaish describes optimism so relentless it seems naive.

polyglot.path: Greek combined poly, many, with glotta, tongue, to describe someone fluent in many languages, literally many-tongued.

polymath.path: Greek polymathes combined poly, many, with manthanein, to learn, describing someone whose knowledge spans many fields.

parts.meaning: solemn procession, escort (from pempein, to send)

pomp.path: Greek pompe named a solemn processional escort. English kept the sense of grand ceremonial display, pomp and circumstance.

pomposity.path: Sharing its root with pomp, grand procession, pomposity is self-importance paraded the way a procession parades splendor.

pompous.path: Pompous shares its root with pomp, a grand procession. A pompous person parades their own importance the way a ceremony parades splendor.

ponderous.path: Latin pondus meant weight. Something ponderous is so heavy, in body or in style, that it moves and unfolds slowly and laboriously.

parts.meaning: high priest (traditionally 'bridge-builder', pons + facere, though this derivation is disputed)

pontifical.literal: of a high priest or pope
pontifical.path: A pontifex was Rome's high priest, an office later given to the Pope, or pontiff. Pontifical first meant relating to a pope or bishop, then broadened to speech delivered with that same self-important, decree-like authority.

pontificate.literal: to act as a high priest
pontificate.path: Pontificate originally meant to perform the office of a bishop or pope. It came to describe anyone who lays down opinions with that same self-important, priestly authority.

populist.path: Latin populus meant the people as a whole. A populist appeals directly to ordinary people, positioning themselves against elites.

porous.path: Greek poros meant a passage or channel. Something porous is riddled with tiny passages that let liquid or air pass through.

portend.path: Latin portendere meant to stretch forth or point out in advance. To portend something is to extend a sign of what is coming.
